name: Alcohol

primary_targets: nAChR (α7, α4β2 inhibition at intox conc.)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Whole-cell patch; ~50 mM ethanol gives ~50% inhibition of NMDA-evoked current; effect is NOT voltage-dependent (so not Mg2+ pore-block-like).
binding.notes: Lovinger, White, Weight 1989, Science 243:1721 — landmark paper. ~50 mM corresponds to ~0.23 g/dL BAC, achievable in heavy drinkers.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Potentiation observed at concentrations as low as 1–3 mM (~5–15 mg/dL BAC) at δ-containing extrasynaptic receptors — controversial; many labs failed to replicate.
binding.notes: Wallner, Hanchar, Olsen 2003. Sensitivity at δ-subunit receptors is disputed; later studies (Borghese et al. 2006, pmid:16921002) failed to replicate the effect, suggesting it requires specific assay conditions.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ethanol potentiates glycine-evoked Cl- current; effect mapped to residues in TM2/TM3 (S267, A52). Mihic, Whiting, Harris 1997 Nature 389:385.
binding.notes: Mihic-Harris site — alcohol pocket in TM2/3 confirmed by mutagenesis.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lovinger, White 1991 — ethanol 25-200 mM potentiates 5-HT-evoked cation current 2-3x.
binding.notes: Underlies emetic and reinforcing effects; ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) reduces alcohol craving in early-onset alcoholics.

functional.notes: Synaptic α1β2γ2 receptors are RELATIVELY ethanol-insensitive (require >60 mM, supra-lethal); the behaviourally relevant GABA-A potentiation appears mediated by extrasynaptic δ-subunit receptors AND by indirect mechanisms (allopregnanolone release, GABA release from interneurons via 5-HT3).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Multi-target depressant. Direct effects: NMDA antagonism (50 mM IC50), glycine PAM, GABA-A δ-subunit PAM at low conc, 5-HT3 PAM. Indirect: ethanol induces neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) synthesis via HPA axis activation, and allopregnanolone is a much more potent GABA-A PAM (nM) than ethanol itself — this neurosteroid loop explains why GABA-A involvement persists at conc where direct ethanol PAM is undetectable. Chronic exposure → adaptive NMDA upregulation (NR2B subunit), GABA-A α4/γ2 switching, and cAMP/PKA signalling rearrangement, all of which underlie tolerance and the withdrawal/seizure phenotype.

neuroimaging.finding: Acute alcohol (0.75 g/kg) increases [11C]raclopride displacement in ventral striatum, indicating ~5-15% dopamine release — much smaller than psychostimulants.
Increased low-frequency (delta/theta) power and reduced alpha at BAC ~0.05-0.10 g/dL. Chronic alcoholics show reduced P300 amplitude (endophenotype for AUD risk).

routes.subject_demographics: Mixed populations; Vd ~0.55 L/kg males, ~0.50 L/kg females (less body water).
routes.notes: Zero-order elimination via ADH (Km ~0.1 g/L = ~2 mM; saturated above ~0.02 g/dL BAC). Elimination rate ~0.015 g/dL/h (range 0.010-0.025); 4-5x higher when CYP2E1 is induced in chronic heavy drinkers. F% reduced by first-pass gastric ADH (~10-25%). Tmax 30-90 min on empty stomach, 60-180 min with food.

concentration_effect.notes: 0.02 BAC = subtle effects; 0.05 = impairment; 0.08 = legal intoxication; 0.30 = stupor; 0.40 = LD50 (untreated); >0.50 typically fatal but tolerance changes this.

metabolism.notes: ADH1B*2 (Arg47His) variant common in East Asians — ~40x faster Vmax → acetaldehyde flush; ADH1B*3 (Arg369Cys) in African ancestry. Acetaldehyde is the toxic intermediate responsible for the disulfiram-like reaction, mutagenicity, and hangover.
ALDH2*2 (Glu487Lys) — homozygotes have <10% enzyme activity, severe acetaldehyde accumulation; ~30-50% of East Asians carry at least one *2 allele. Strong protection against alcoholism.

Low-affinity (Km ~10 mM) but inducible up to 10x by chronic ethanol — explains accelerated clearance in heavy drinkers and increased hepatotoxicity (CYP2E1 generates ROS). Disulfiram is a mechanism-based CYP2E1 inactivator (its metabolite DDC).
Brain catalase pathway contributes to central ethanol metabolism and may be relevant to behavioural effects (acetaldehyde in CNS is rewarding).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Acetaldehyde accumulates 5-10x → flushing, tachycardia, vomiting, hypotension. Onset within 10 min, lasts hours. Inhibition irreversible — effect persists ~1-2 wks after last disulfiram dose.
Disulfiram-like flushing reaction with ethanol co-ingestion.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: CYP2E1 induction shifts paracetamol metabolism toward toxic NAPQI metabolite; glutathione depletion in chronic drinkers
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased hepatotoxicity risk at supratherapeutic paracetamol doses in chronic alcohol users.
Marked respiratory depression risk; common cause of accidental overdose death.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: ADH1B*2 (rs1229984, Arg47His) — ~40x increased Vmax, common in East Asians, protective against AUD. ALDH2*2 (rs671, Glu487Lys) — heterozygotes ~30% activity, homozygotes ~0%; strong AUD protection via flush. CYP2E1*5B (c1/c2) — moderately inducible variant, weak AUD association.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-A α1 downregulation and α4/γ2 upregulation in chronic exposure (rats, weeks); NMDA NR2B upregulation drives kindling and withdrawal seizures.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 6-24 h after last drink. Mild: tremor, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity (peak 24-48 h). Severe: seizures (peak 24-48 h, occur in 5-15% of dependent withdrawers without prophylaxis), delirium tremens (onset 48-96 h, mortality 5% treated / 35% untreated). Driven by NMDA upregulation + GABA-A downregulation. Benzodiazepine cover (CIWA-Ar protocol) is the standard of care.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Direct GIRK potentiation contributes to GABA-B-like analgesia and sedation at high doses.
Cross-talk with nicotine reward circuitry; partly underlies the alcohol-tobacco co-use epidemiology.

demographic_differences.sex: Women reach ~30-40% higher peak BAC for same dose/kg due to lower body water (Vd ~0.49 vs 0.55 L/kg) and lower gastric ADH activity (~40% lower first-pass).
demographic_differences.age: Elderly have ~10-20% lower Vd and slower elimination; teens have higher tolerance to motor effects but equal or greater impairment of memory.
demographic_differences.weight: Standard dose calc uses Widmark formula: BAC = dose(g) / (Vd(L/kg) × body weight(kg)).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Cirrhosis prolongs elimination by ~50% and disrupts the ADH/ALDH ratio toward acetaldehyde accumulation.

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative cross-talk between ethanol PAM and neurosteroid pathway in humans
notes: The 'GABA-A potentiator' label is correct but misleading — ethanol's direct GABA-A effects require >>10 mM at synaptic receptors; the behaviourally relevant GABA enhancement is mostly via neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) induction. NMDA antagonism dominates at typical intoxicating BACs.

name: GHB

binding.target: GHB-specific high-affinity binding site (distinct from GABA-B)
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Maitre lab — multiple papers from 1980s identifying stereoselective, saturable binding distinct from GABA-B. NCS-382 (Maitre 1990) is the selective antagonist (Ki ~340 nM) that does NOT bind GABA-B.
binding.notes: Castelli et al. 2004 (Neurosci Lett) — confirmed by molecular evidence that [3H]GHB does NOT bind HEK293 expressing GABA-B R1/R2. Identity of the GHB receptor cloned in 2003 (Andriamampandry, Maitre — pmid:14555562) as GPR172A is contested; the true molecular identity remains uncertain.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lingenhoehl et al. 1999 (pmid:10591456) — GHB is a low-potency weak partial agonist at GABA-B (EC50 ~150-500 μM, Emax ~25-30% of baclofen). At clinically achieved brain conc. (~250-500 μM at recreational doses) GHB activates GABA-B sufficiently to produce sedation and respiratory depression — GABA-B is the target responsible for the intoxicating effects.
binding.notes: CRITICAL: low-dose GHB (~10-30 mg/kg) reaches conc that activates only the high-affinity GHB receptor → mild stimulation, euphoria. High-dose (>50 mg/kg) GHB reaches ~250-500 μM and engages GABA-B → sedation, coma. This biphasic dose-response is mechanistically explained by the two binding sites.

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 + Xenopus oocytes expressing human α4β3δ
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Absalom et al. 2012 — GHB is a low-potency (EC50 ~140 μM) but quite efficacious agonist at α4β1δ and α4β3δ GABA-A; partial inverse agonism at α4β3γ2 at higher conc. δ-selective effect parallels neurosteroid pharmacology.
binding.notes: PNAS paper proposes that δ-GABA-A contributes to GHB's absence-seizure liability and to the dose-dependent switch from euphoria to sedation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual-receptor model: at low brain concentrations (<100 μM) GHB selectively activates the high-affinity GHB receptor (Maitre receptor) which produces dopamine modulation and the stimulatory/pro-cognitive low-dose effects observed in rodents and at sub-medical doses in humans. At high brain concentrations (>200 μM, reached at recreational/medical Xyrem doses) GABA-B activation dominates → GIRK opening → hyperpolarisation, ↓cAMP, sedation, GH release, respiratory depression. The δ-GABA-A activation at ~140 μM may contribute to absence-seizure-like EEG and the deep stage-3/4 sleep pattern seen with Xyrem.

neuroimaging.finding: Xyrem (sodium oxybate) increases slow-wave sleep (N3) duration and amplitude in narcolepsy; produces 2.5-3 Hz spike-wave discharges (absence-like) in some species at supratherapeutic doses.

routes.subject_demographics: Brenneisen et al. 2004 healthy volunteers, 25 mg/kg PO; t1/2 = 30.4 ± 2.45 min, Vd 52.7 ± 15 L.
routes.notes: F% low (~25%) due to extensive first-pass and pre-systemic decarboxylation; absorption AND elimination are capacity-limited — doubling dose more than doubles AUC and Cmax. Food reduces Cmax by ~70%. Within the recreational dose range, half-life lengthens from ~30 min (low dose) to ~60-90 min (high dose) as metabolism saturates.

concentration_effect.notes: Couper & Logan: plasma >50 mg/L drowsiness; >150 mg/L unconsciousness; >250 mg/L deep coma. Toxic range overlaps recreational range — narrow therapeutic index.

metabolism.notes: GHB → SSA → succinate → CO2 + H2O. Endogenous pathway, saturable (Km ~50-100 μM). β-oxidation pathway also contributes. Renal excretion of unchanged GHB <5%.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic: shared GABA-B and respiratory depression; ethanol also competes for ADH/aldehyde dehydrogenase
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Marked synergistic respiratory depression; ethanol prolongs GHB half-life ~30%.
Markedly elevated GHB AUC and prolonged half-life; contraindicated with Xyrem.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: SSADH deficiency (Aldh5a1 -/-) accumulates GHB and GABA, causing intellectual disability and seizures — illustrates the saturable metabolism vulnerability.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Chronic GHB → GABA-B receptor desensitization and downregulation (rodent studies); contributes to severe withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1-6 h after last dose (very short — driven by short t1/2). Mild: tremor, anxiety, insomnia, tachycardia. Severe: delirium, psychosis, hallucinations, autonomic instability — closely resembles severe alcohol/benzo withdrawal; can be life-threatening. Treatment: high-dose benzodiazepines + baclofen + sometimes phenobarbital. The protracted course (psychiatric sequelae weeks-to-months) is attributed to GABA-B receptor downregulation.

off_targets.target: endogenous opioid release (dopamine via GABA-B disinhibition)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Reinforcing properties partly opioid-mediated; naloxone partially blocks GHB-induced dopamine release in some studies.

demographic_differences.sex: Females may have higher GHB AUC than males at same mg/kg (rat data); limited human evidence.
demographic_differences.weight: Dose typically scaled to lean body mass given low Vd (~0.4 L/kg) and dose-dependent kinetics.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment prolongs t1/2; renal excretion minimal so renal failure has little effect on parent GHB.

data_gaps_remaining: Molecular identity of the high-affinity GHB receptor in humans (GPR172A controversial)
Quantitative human PK-PD model for narrow therapeutic window
notes: The dual-receptor pharmacology (high-affinity GHB receptor at low doses; GABA-B at high doses) is the single most important and most-overlooked fact about this compound. Maitre's group (Strasbourg, 1980s-2000s) did the foundational work characterising the GHB-specific binding site; Couper & Logan provided forensic concentration-effect data.

name: GBL

primary_targets: GHB (via rapid in vivo lactonase hydrolysis)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: GBL itself is essentially inactive at GHB/GABA-B; its effects derive from peripheral and tissue-lactonase conversion to GHB.
binding.notes: Lettieri & Fung 1979; Roth & Giarman 1968. The lactone form is extremely lipophilic → faster absorption and more rapid onset than equimolar GHB. F% approaches 100% (vs 25% for GHB) due to bypass of first-pass GHB-saturable metabolism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See GHB. GBL is a prodrug; the half-life of conversion in human plasma is <1 minute (serum paraoxonase / arylesterase activity). Onset ~5-10 min vs ~20-30 min for GHB.

routes.subject_demographics: Lettieri & Fung 1979 — GBL t1/2 in plasma ~1 min; GHB Cmax higher and Tmax shorter after GBL than equimolar GHB.
routes.notes: Equimolar conversion: 1 mL GBL ≈ 1.6 g GHB equivalent (density 1.13 g/mL, MW 86.1 vs GHB MW 104.1). Faster onset and higher peak make GBL more dangerous than GHB even at 'equivalent' doses.

metabolism.notes: Conversion is essentially complete and very rapid (t1/2 <1 min in plasma at 37°C). All subsequent PK/PD is GHB pharmacology.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major respiratory-depression risk; common in club-drug overdoses.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: PON1 Q192R polymorphism alters lactonase activity — may modestly affect onset speed, but conversion is so fast that polymorphism likely has limited clinical impact.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Identical to GHB withdrawal; often more severe because GBL users dose more frequently (faster onset / shorter perceived effect).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Pure GBL is caustic at high concentrations — oral/oesophageal burns reported with undiluted ingestion.

notes: GBL is operationally indistinguishable from GHB after the first minute, but the faster onset and higher F% make it disproportionately overdose-prone. Per-volume potency is ~1.6x GHB.

name: 1,4-butanediol

binding.assay_buffer_notes: 1,4-BD is converted in two steps: alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) → γ-hydroxybutyraldehyde → aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) → GHB. Both enzymes are the same as for ethanol metabolism.
binding.notes: Onset slower than GHB or GBL (~20-40 min) because of two-step enzymatic conversion. Co-administration with ethanol drastically slows conversion (ADH competitive substrate) → unpredictable, delayed, prolonged effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure prodrug. All effects are GHB-mediated after conversion via ADH/ALDH.

routes.notes: Pharmacokinetics governed by ADH Km (saturable) — like ethanol, exhibits zero-order conversion at high doses. Equimolar potency to GHB. Ethanol co-ingestion → ADH competition → delayed and unpredictable onset, can cause stacking overdoses.

metabolism.notes: Competition with ethanol at ADH explains the well-documented danger of mixing BD with alcohol.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Competitive ADH inhibition → delayed conversion to GHB; ethanol metabolism wins, BD pools
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Delayed/prolonged sedation, re-dosing risk, increased overdose deaths.
Blocks BD → GHB conversion; theoretical antidote for BD overdose although clinical evidence sparse.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: ALDH2*2 variant would cause aldehyde intermediate accumulation; potentially severe flush-like reaction.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Aldehyde intermediate may contribute to hepatotoxicity with repeated use; less well characterised than GHB.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment slows conversion; renal impairment slows GHB excretion.

notes: Slowest-onset GHB prodrug due to two enzymatic conversion steps. Co-ingestion with ethanol is uniquely dangerous because the ADH bottleneck causes BD to accumulate then release as ethanol clears.

name: Aceburic acid

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acetyl ester of GHB; hydrolysed by carboxylesterases to release GHB. No direct receptor pharmacology described.

routes.notes: No published human PK data; treated as a GHB prodrug by analogy.

metabolism.notes: Inferred by chemical analogy.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Same as GHB if used chronically.

data_gaps_remaining: All human PK and PD data
notes: Obscure GHB prodrug; no significant clinical or research literature beyond the substance ID.

name: Gabapentin

primary_targets: α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Suman-Chauhan et al. 1993 — original characterisation of the α2δ binding site. Gomez et al. confirmed in recombinant α2δ-1: Kd ~59 nM at α2δ-1 vs 153 nM at α2δ-2.
binding.notes: Note: NOT a GABA receptor ligand despite the name. Does NOT bind GABA-A, GABA-B, or GABA-T. Therapeutic effect via Cav α2δ-1 binding → reduced trafficking of Cav2.1/2.2 to presynaptic terminals → ↓glutamate release. Effect manifests over hours-days, not seconds.

functional.notes: Reduces stimulated glutamate release ~25-40%; effect requires hours-days of treatment, reflecting reduced trafficking of α2δ-1-containing Cav channels to the membrane rather than acute channel block.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds α2δ-1 → disrupts trafficking and surface expression of Cav2.1/Cav2.2 at presynaptic terminals → reduced glutamate, noradrenaline, substance P release at hyperexcitable synapses. Also disrupts α2δ-1 / thrombospondin interaction (Eroglu 2009) → modulates excitatory synaptogenesis in development. The slow onset of analgesic/anxiolytic effect (days-weeks) reflects these trafficking and structural mechanisms.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults; PK is dose-dependent due to saturable LAT1 absorption.
routes.notes: F% drops from ~60% at 300 mg → ~47% at 600 mg → ~34% at 1200 mg → ~25% at 3600 mg due to saturation of LAT1 (SLC7A5, L-type amino acid transporter) in gut. t1/2 5-7 h (longer in renal failure: CL closely tracks CrCl). Negligible protein binding. ~100% renally excreted unchanged.

concentration_effect.notes: Therapeutic range approximate; no formal therapeutic drug monitoring established.

metabolism.notes: Excreted essentially unchanged in urine. No CYP involvement. No drug-drug interactions via CYP.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Separate doses by ≥2 h.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic synergy at respiratory depression; mild PK interaction (morphine ↑gabapentin AUC ~44%)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major OD-risk amplifier — multiple coronial reports of gabapentinoid-opioid combined deaths.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: LAT1 polymorphisms may explain inter-individual variability in F% (~20-30%) but no clinically validated genotype guidance.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Long-term gabapentin increases α2δ-1 expression in some animal models — possible mechanism for tolerance and rebound hyperalgesia.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-48 h after abrupt discontinuation. Anxiety, insomnia, GI upset, diaphoresis, tachycardia; case reports of seizures, particularly in patients with epilepsy or co-existing AUD/BZ dependence. Less severe than benzodiazepine or phenibut withdrawal but real.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Disruption of excitatory synaptogenesis — relevant to in-utero exposure and developing CNS.

demographic_differences.sex: No major sex difference in PK.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced proportional to renal function; dose-adjust by CrCl.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: CrCl <60: reduce dose; CrCl <15: 100-300 mg/day. Hepatic impairment irrelevant (no metabolism).

notes: The name 'gabapentin' is misleading — it has no direct action at any GABA receptor. The mechanism is Cav α2δ-1 binding with downstream effects on glutamate (not GABA) release. Saturable LAT1 absorption makes dose-response flatten at high doses.

name: Pregabalin

primary_targets: α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

binding.tissue_or_cell: recombinant human α2δ-1 in baculovirus-infected Sf9 cells
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Belliotti et al. 2005, Bian et al. 2006 — pregabalin Ki 32 nM at α2δ-1 (~6x higher affinity than gabapentin Ki ~140 nM). Kd 6.0 nM in direct binding.
binding.notes: (S)-enantiomer is active; (R) is inactive.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Pregabalin nearly equipotent at α2δ-1 vs α2δ-2 (Kd 6 vs 7 nM); gabapentin shows ~3x α2δ-1 preference.

functional.notes: Reduces stimulated transmitter release ~30-50% (Dooley et al. 2007).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same mechanism as gabapentin (Cav α2δ binding → reduced trafficking → reduced presynaptic Ca2+ entry → reduced glutamate/NA/Sub-P release at hyperexcitable terminals). Pregabalin's ~6x higher α2δ-1 affinity translates to lower mg doses and a more rapid onset of clinical effect than gabapentin.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults; PK linear up to clinical doses (LAT1 not saturated at standard 150-600 mg/d).
routes.notes: Bioavailability ~90% (higher than gabapentin because pregabalin uses multiple transporters in addition to LAT1). PK linear, predictable. t1/2 6.3 h. Renal excretion ~98% unchanged. No food effect on AUC.

concentration_effect.notes: Approximate; clinical response is dose-rather-than-conc guided.

metabolism.notes: <2% metabolised. ~98% renally excreted unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Coronial data show pregabalin involved in ~10-25% of opioid overdose deaths in regions with high prescription; UK reclassified as Schedule 3 controlled drug in 2019.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-72 h. Anxiety, insomnia, autonomic activation, occasionally seizures and psychosis. More severe than gabapentin withdrawal due to higher α2δ affinity and shorter t1/2. Particularly difficult in patients with co-existing BZ/AUD dependence.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Strictly renal dosing required. CrCl 30-60: half dose; CrCl <30: quarter dose.

notes: Higher α2δ affinity (~6x) and predictable linear PK distinguish pregabalin from gabapentin. Higher abuse and overdose liability than gabapentin in surveillance data.

name: Phenibut

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Zvejniece et al. 2015 — R-phenibut Ki 23 μM; S-phenibut 39 μM; baclofen 156 μM; gabapentin 50 nM. R-phenibut is the active enantiomer for α2δ binding (~7000x weaker than gabapentin but pharmacologically relevant at high mg doses).
binding.notes: Key paper. R-phenibut also produces gabapentin-like anti-nociceptive effects in mice.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lapin 2001 review of Soviet/post-Soviet work. R-phenibut is the active enantiomer; S-phenibut shows little GABA-B activity. EC50 in μM range, Emax ~30-50% of baclofen at GABA-B.
binding.notes: Original characterization by Khaunina & Lapin 1976 (Soviet literature, untranslated).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual mechanism: GABA-B partial agonism (anxiolysis, sedation, prolactin/GH release) + α2δ-1 binding (anti-nociceptive, sleep). The combination produces a phenibut phenotype distinct from either pure GABA-B agonist (baclofen) or pure α2δ ligand (gabapentin). Severe withdrawal is attributed to GABA-B receptor downregulation analogous to GHB.

routes.subject_demographics: Limited Soviet PK data (single study cited in WHO 2021 pre-review). 65% excreted unchanged in urine.
routes.notes: t1/2 ~5.3 h. Reportedly only ~0.1% reaches brain. Crosses placenta and BBB. Limited modern PK literature.

metabolism.notes: ~65% urinary unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic synergy at GABA-B and respiratory centres
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major respiratory depression / sedation risk.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-B receptor downregulation occurs within weeks of daily use (rodent and clinical inference); recovery may take weeks to months — explains the protracted withdrawal seen clinically.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-48 h after last dose. Severe: anxiety, agitation, psychomotor activation, insomnia, hallucinations, psychosis, autonomic instability, occasionally seizures. Duration 2-4 weeks with protracted PAWS up to months. Closely resembles GHB and severe BZ withdrawal. Treatment: baclofen tapers ± benzodiazepines; multiple Baltic/Russian case reports document the syndrome (Ahuja 2018, Hardman 2019, Magsalin 2018, Joshi 2017).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: increased CNS sensitivity; reduce dose.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal impairment likely prolongs t1/2 (predominantly renal excretion).

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative human PK; clinical brain conc-effect relationships
notes: The withdrawal syndrome described by Magsalin & Khan 2014, Hardman 2019, Ahuja 2018 in English-language case series and earlier in untranslated Baltic/Russian literature is mechanistically explained by GABA-B receptor downregulation — analogous to GHB protracted withdrawal. Phenibut is the only dual GABA-B + α2δ ligand in widespread non-medical use.

name: 4-Fluorophenibut

binding.target: GABA-B + α2δ-1 (rat brain) — by close analogy to phenibut
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Fluorine substitution at para-position of phenyl ring typically increases lipophilicity (logP ~0.5 higher), CNS penetration, and metabolic stability vs phenibut. Often anecdotally reported as 2-5x more potent than phenibut.
binding.notes: No peer-reviewed Ki/EC50 published.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Inferred analogous to phenibut (GABA-B partial agonism + α2δ ligand).

routes.notes: No formal human PK; user reports suggest longer duration than phenibut (8-16 h) consistent with fluorine-induced metabolic stabilisation.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe phenibut-like withdrawal reported in case series.

notes: RC analogue of phenibut. Same dual GABA-B + α2δ mechanism inferred but no formal pharmacology characterization in peer-reviewed literature. The 'Fluorophenibut' entry is a duplicate.

name: F-Phenibut

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 4-Fluorophenibut (same molecule, duplicate entry).

notes: Duplicate library entry for 4-Fluorophenibut. Consolidate.

name: Fluorophenibut

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 4-Fluorophenibut.

notes: Duplicate library entry for 4-Fluorophenibut.

name: Baclofen

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Classical value from Bowery 1980s. Recombinant hR1a/R1b receptors give higher EC50s (~30 μM) — discrepancy attributed to lack of native receptor accessory proteins (KCTD subunits) in recombinant systems.
binding.notes: R-baclofen is the active enantiomer (~50-200x more potent than S).

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells expressing human GABA-B R1a/R2 coupled to Kir3.1/3.2
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Liu et al. 2004 — EC50 11.3 μM at hR1a/R2 + Kir3.1/3.2 channels. Differs from native receptor EC50 by ~100x, illustrating the role of accessory subunits.
binding.notes: Reference agonist for the GABA-B receptor.

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Functional receptor requires both R1 (orthosteric site) and R2 (Gi/o coupling). KCTD8/12/16 cytoplasmic accessory proteins shape kinetics and desensitisation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Gi/o → ↓adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP) + βγ → Kir3 (GIRK) opening (hyperpolarisation) and Cav2.x inhibition (↓presynaptic Ca2+ → ↓transmitter release). Both pre- and postsynaptic actions contribute. Baclofen is the prototype selective GABA-B agonist and the reference for all GABA-B pharmacology.

routes.notes: t1/2 2-6 h. 70-85% renally excreted unchanged. ~15% hepatic deamination.
Intrathecal dosing 1000x lower than oral (~50-800 μg/day vs 30-80 mg/day PO). Bypasses limited BBB penetration.

metabolism.notes: Most clearance is renal of unchanged drug.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Profound CNS / respiratory depression. Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal is a medical emergency (rebound spasticity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis).

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-B desensitisation via KCTD-dependent kinetics; chronic baclofen → tolerance and rebound on abrupt withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 24-72 h after oral discontinuation; faster after pump failure (intrathecal). Severe rebound spasticity, hallucinations, seizures, autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis. Intrathecal withdrawal can be fatal — requires emergency intrathecal restart or oral high-dose substitution.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: increased CNS sensitivity, reduce dose.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: CrCl <60: reduce dose; CrCl <30: marked accumulation, prolonged t1/2 → encephalopathy risk at standard doses.

notes: Reference selective GABA-B agonist. The R1/R2 obligate heterodimer architecture (Marshall & Foord 1998; Pin & Bettler crystal structures) and KCTD accessory subunits are essential for understanding why recombinant Ki values diverge from native-tissue Ki values by 100-1000x.

name: Phenobarbital

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 or Xenopus oocytes expressing human α1β2γ2
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Phenobarbital potentiates GABA-A in 50-500 μM range; at >1 mM activates the channel directly (without GABA). Therapeutic plasma 10-40 μg/mL (43-170 μM) — overlap with potentiation range. Lower direct activation than pentobarbital (less anaesthesia, more anticonvulsant utility).
binding.notes: Reduced propensity to directly activate vs pentobarbital — explains lower anaesthetic potency but acceptable safety margin for chronic anti-epileptic use.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds intersubunit β+/α- pocket in GABA-A TM domain (distinct from BZ site at α/γ interface). Effects on channel: at low conc prolongs mean open time; at high conc directly opens channel without GABA (chloride conductance increase) → this direct gating mode underlies the higher lethality of barbiturates vs benzodiazepines.

routes.notes: Extraordinarily long t1/2 (~4 days) — allows once-daily dosing for epilepsy. ~25-50% renal unchanged; balance hepatic CYP2C9, CYP2C19 oxidation.

metabolism.notes: Also CYP2C19, CYP2E1 minor.

drug_interactions_pk.with: warfarin, oral contraceptives, theophylline, many AEDs
drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Strong pan-CYP induction (CAR/PXR activation) — CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 induced 2-5x
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Markedly reduced exposure of CYP3A/2C substrates; classic inducer.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C9 poor metabolisers (~5% Caucasians) have reduced clearance — risk of accumulation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-A subunit composition shifts with chronic exposure (α1 → α4).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1-3 days (long t1/2 delays). Tremor, anxiety, insomnia, seizures, delirium tremens-like syndrome. Severe; mortality without treatment 5-10%. Phenobarbital itself is used for treating barbiturate, BZ, and alcohol withdrawal due to its long t1/2 and self-tapering kinetics.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Weak inhibition at supratherapeutic conc; contributes minimally to anticonvulsant effect.

demographic_differences.age: Neonates: very long t1/2 (~100 h); elderly: prolonged.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Dose-adjust for renal failure (25-50% renal); hepatic impairment may slow metabolism.

notes: Less direct GABA-A channel activation than pentobarbital → better therapeutic index for chronic epilepsy use. Classic CAR/PXR-mediated CYP inducer (predates the cloning of nuclear receptors — 'phenobarbital induction' was the prototype).

name: Pentobarbital

primary_targets: GABA-A (β-subunit barbiturate pocket; direct agonist at high conc.)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Steinbach lab: pentobarbital ~50-100 μM PAM; ~500 μM direct agonist (channel opening without GABA). Plasma anaesthetic conc 20-50 μg/mL (~80-200 μM) — overlap with both modes.
binding.notes: The direct agonist mode (channel opens with no GABA) is the property that makes barbiturates more lethal than benzos — overdose produces sustained chloride conductance independent of endogenous GABA tone, → flat-line EEG, respiratory arrest.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same site as phenobarbital but with higher direct-activation efficacy → anaesthesia. Used for euthanasia in veterinary/MAID contexts because of predictable, rapid, deep anaesthesia followed by respiratory arrest.

routes.notes: t1/2 15-50 h. Hepatic oxidation (CYP3A4, CYP2C19) → inactive metabolites. <1% renal unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Similar pan-inducer profile to phenobarbital, less studied.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe — seizures, delirium; treated with substitution and taper.

notes: Higher direct-channel-opening efficacy than phenobarbital explains its preferential use for anaesthesia and euthanasia.

name: Methaqualone

primary_targets: GABA-A (transmembrane β+/α- intersubunit site; etomidate-like pocket)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Hammer et al. 2015 — methaqualone PAM at α1,2,3,5β2,3γ2S with EC50 ~1-10 μM. Diverse functionalities at α4,6β1,2,3δ subtypes ranging from inactive → negative AM → positive AM → super-agonist.
binding.notes: Binding site distinct from BZ and barbiturate sites — overlaps with etomidate/propofol intersubunit transmembrane site. Crystal structure: methaqualone widens TM2 ion-conducting pore.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: GABA-A PAM at the propofol/etomidate pocket. Quinazolinone scaffold inserts deeper into subunit interface than BZ-site ligands.

routes.notes: t1/2 20-60 h. Extensive hepatic hydroxylation (CYP3A4 likely). Lipophilic, large Vd.

notes: Hammer 2015 (Mol Pharmacol) is the definitive modern characterisation. The etomidate-site binding distinguishes it from BZ and barbiturate-site modulators.

name: Barbital

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Long-acting barbiturate; weaker direct GABA-A gating than pentobarbital but similar site. Very long t1/2 (~50-100 h). Historical first synthetic hypnotic (1903).

routes.notes: Largely renal excretion (~70-90% unchanged) due to low lipophilicity.

metabolism.notes: Mostly excreted unchanged.

notes: Historic; rarely used clinically since the 1950s.

name: Amobarbital

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Intermediate-acting barbiturate; t1/2 ~20-25 h. Mechanism: GABA-A PAM with high-conc direct activation (typical barbiturate).

routes.notes: Hepatic hydroxylation.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Pan-CYP induction like other barbiturates.

notes: 'Truth serum' historical use due to disinhibition at sub-anaesthetic doses.

name: Secobarbital

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Short-to-intermediate-acting barbiturate; faster onset and offset than amobarbital (allyl + sec-pentyl side chains increase lipophilicity).

routes.notes: Used in MAID protocols (Switzerland, Belgium, Oregon).

notes: Classic 'rainbow' Tuinal component (with amobarbital).

name: Thiopental

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thiobarbiturate — sulfur substitution at C2 increases lipophilicity and rapid CNS onset. Used for induction of general anaesthesia (IV). Ultra-short clinical effect (5-10 min) due to redistribution rather than metabolism.

routes.subject_demographics: Adults; t1/2β 11 h but clinical recovery <10 min due to peripheral redistribution.
routes.notes: Classic 'context-sensitive half-life' demonstration drug — single dose is short due to redistribution; infusions accumulate dramatically.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment prolongs offset; obese patients accumulate due to large lipid Vd.

notes: Withdrawn from US market 2011 (manufacturer cited execution-protocol concerns).

name: Allobarbital

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Intermediate-acting barbiturate (1922). Mechanism by class.

notes: Largely historic.

name: Hexobarbital

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Short-acting barbiturate. Historic. R-(–)-hexobarbital and S-(+)-hexobarbital are pharmacokinetically distinct (CYP2C19 probe drug — hexobarbital hydroxylation was a classical CYP2C19 phenotyping assay).

routes.notes: Marked stereoselective PK: R-enantiomer cleared ~3x faster than S by CYP2C19.

metabolism.notes: Classical CYP2C19 probe.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs have markedly prolonged sleep duration after hexobarbital — landmark observation of pharmacogenetic clinical relevance.

notes: Important historical role establishing CYP2C19 polymorphism's clinical effect.

name: Tuinal

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Fixed-ratio combination capsule: secobarbital sodium + amobarbital sodium 1:1. Discontinued. See individual entries.

notes: Combination product; see secobarbital and amobarbital entries.

name: Propofol

primary_targets: GABA-A (β-subunit intersubunit transmembrane pocket; β3 critical)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Olsen 2018 review and Cohen 2014 (PMC3951778) — labels β-M286 at the β+/α- intersubunit transmembrane site. β3-N265M mutation abolishes anaesthesia in mice (Jurd 2003).
binding.notes: Photolabelling identifies multiple binding sites; β+/α- pocket dominant for anaesthetic effect.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: GABA-A PAM at the etomidate-/methaqualone-overlap β+/α- site. At anaesthetic conc directly opens the channel without GABA. Other minor targets: glycine PAM, nAChR inhibition, Na+ channel inhibition, sphingosine-1-phosphate-like signalling reported.

neuroimaging.finding: Frontal alpha (8-12 Hz) coherence increase and slow-delta dominance characteristic of propofol unconsciousness — Purdon spectrogram signature.

routes.notes: Three-compartment model. Rapid distribution t1/2α 2-4 min, redistribution t1/2β 30-70 min, terminal t1/2γ 4-12 h. Context-sensitive half-life ~25 min even after 8-h infusion — major advantage over thiopental. Hepatic + extrahepatic CL exceeds liver blood flow (extra-hepatic clearance, ~30% of total).

metabolism.notes: Major pathway.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6*6 reduces propofol metabolism modestly; not routinely actioned.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Withdrawal not described in normal use; abuse-related dependence reported in anaesthesia providers (occupational risk).

off_targets.target: PRIS — propofol infusion syndrome (mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation impairment)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure with prolonged high-dose (>4 mg/kg/h >48 h) infusion.

demographic_differences.sex: Women: ~30% faster recovery; pharmacokinetic differences modest.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: 30-50% dose reduction (slower CL + increased CNS sensitivity).
demographic_differences.weight: Lean body mass for dosing in obesity.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment has surprisingly little PK impact (extrahepatic CL); renal failure does not require dose adjustment.

notes: The β3-N265M knock-in mouse experiments (Jurd 2003) genetically prove β3-containing GABA-A as the anaesthetic target. Distinct β3 vs β2 selectivity from etomidate.

name: Chloral Hydrate

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Trichloroethanol (TCE) — the active metabolite — potentiates GABA-A currents at the barbiturate site (Lovinger & Peoples).
binding.notes: Chloral hydrate itself is essentially a prodrug for TCE.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug → TCE via ADH (very rapid, t1/2 minutes). TCE is the active GABA-A PAM and also a TTX-resistant Na+ channel modulator (BMC Anesth 2023). Chloral hydrate is genotoxic in itself (formaldehyde-like aldehyde) — chronic use linked to hepatic/renal toxicity.

routes.notes: Chloral hydrate t1/2 in plasma ~4 min (rapid ADH conversion). Active TCE t1/2 dominates clinical effect.

metabolism.notes: TCE is more potent than parent; UGT2B7 glucuronidation is rate-limiting for elimination.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 'Mickey Finn' — alcohol slows TCE clearance and TCE displaces ethanol from albumin → marked sedation.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: TCE displaces warfarin from albumin → transient INR increase
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Transient anticoagulant potentiation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Chronic exposure linked to liver tumors in rodents; IARC Group 2A.

demographic_differences.age: Withdrawn for paediatric use in many countries due to genotoxicity concerns.

notes: Classical 'knockout drops' (Mickey Finn). Mostly replaced by BZs and other sedatives. TCE is the relevant pharmacologically active species.

name: Noctec

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trade name for chloral hydrate.

notes: Trade name duplicate — see Chloral Hydrate.

name: Chloral-betaine

primary_targets: GABA-A (via TCE, after chloral hydrate release)
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Complex of chloral hydrate with betaine — gastric dissociation releases chloral hydrate. All subsequent PK/PD is chloral-hydrate pharmacology.

notes: Adduct formulation intended to reduce gastric irritation. Long withdrawn.

name: Glutethimide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Piperidine-dione hypnotic. Anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, mydriasis) distinguish from pure barbiturates. Strong CYP induction (CAR/PXR). Classic 'doors and fours' polydrug (with codeine).

routes.notes: Erratic absorption; saturable, food-affected. t1/2 8-12 h. Active hydroxylated metabolite (4-hydroxyglutethimide).

metabolism.notes: Active metabolite implicated in delayed coma after overdose.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced anticoagulation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Mydriasis distinguishes overdose from other sedatives.

notes: Withdrawn most markets. Notable for delayed overdose presentation (active metabolite).

name: Methyprylon

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Piperidine-dione hypnotic similar to glutethimide; withdrawn.

notes: Withdrawn 1965.

name: Placdyl

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ethchlorvynol — tertiary alcohol hypnotic. GABA-A PAM at a site overlapping the alcohol/anaesthetic pocket. Severe overdose has prolonged coma (5-15 days). Withdrawn 1999.

routes.notes: Biphasic, two-compartment; lipid sequestration explains prolonged coma.

notes: Withdrawn.

name: Carisoprodol

primary_targets: GABA-A (barbiturate-like PAM, partly via meprobamate metabolite)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Gonzalez et al. 2009: carisoprodol potentiates and directly gates GABA-A in a barbiturate-like manner (EC50 ~480 μM PAM; ~3 mM direct activation). Meprobamate metabolite contributes substantially to abuse liability.
binding.notes: PMC2858432 — 'Abuse Potential of Soma: the GABA-A Receptor as a Target' is the modern definitive characterisation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Direct GABA-A PAM (and at high conc, direct gating) + meprobamate (an active anxiolytic metabolite at GABA-A). Combined pharmacology underlies muscle relaxation, anxiolysis, and abuse potential.

routes.subject_demographics: Adults. t1/2 carisoprodol 1-2 h; meprobamate metabolite t1/2 6-17 h.
routes.notes: CYP2C19 PMs: 4x parent exposure, 50% less meprobamate — abuse pattern differs by genotype.

metabolism.notes: Meprobamate is the major anxiolytic metabolite; itself was a marketed drug (Miltown, withdrawn for abuse).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased sedation from parent; reduced anxiolytic efficacy.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CPIC-grade pharmacogenetic effect: PMs have 4x carisoprodol exposure and 50% reduced meprobamate.

notes: The CYP2C19 pharmacogenetic dimension is unusual and clinically meaningful — PMs get more direct sedation, EMs get more meprobamate-mediated anxiolysis.

name: Cyclobenzaprine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Cyclobenzaprine is structurally a tricyclic (amitriptyline analogue with cycloheptatriene bridge); affinity profile overlaps with TCA receptor pattern.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 5-HT2A antagonism at brainstem reticular formation reduces α-motoneuron tone — primary mechanism of muscle relaxation. NOT a true muscle relaxant (no direct neuromuscular junction effect). Anticholinergic, antihistaminic, anti-α1 effects underlie side effects.

routes.notes: t1/2 18 h. Extensive first-pass (F ~33-55%). Hepatic CYP3A4/CYP1A2/CYP2D6 metabolism + glucuronidation.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome risk; contraindicated.

off_targets.target: Na+ channels (sodium-channel block at supratherapeutic conc.)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: TCA-like cardiotoxicity in overdose (QRS widening).

notes: Structurally a TCA (amitriptyline analogue); shares cardiac sodium-channel risk in overdose.

name: Metaxalone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Central muscle relaxant; specific receptor target not definitively identified. Less sedating than cyclobenzaprine; minimal anticholinergic activity.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~9 h. Food markedly increases F% (~50% Cmax increase).

notes: Mechanism truly not well-characterised.

name: Quetiapine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Goldstein 2005 — H1 affinity drives the dominant sedative effect at low doses (25-100 mg), explaining the widespread off-label sleep use.
Low D2 affinity + fast dissociation explain antipsychotic efficacy at 300+ mg but minimal EPS.

binding.notes: Drives orthostatic hypotension.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Low-dose pharmacology (25-200 mg) is dominated by H1 and α1 antagonism → sedation, hypotension. Antipsychotic effect requires ≥300 mg for sufficient D2 occupancy. Norquetiapine (active metabolite, CYP3A4-generated) is a potent NET inhibitor (Ki ~12 nM) and 5-HT1A partial agonist — contributes to antidepressant/anxiolytic effects at higher doses.

neuroimaging.finding: D2 occupancy 12-44% at 150-750 mg; 5-HT2A occupancy >80% at 300+ mg.

routes.subject_demographics: Adults; t1/2 6-7 h IR, 7-13 h XR.
routes.notes: Extensive hepatic CYP3A4. F% well-absorbed; food has minor effect.

metabolism.notes: Norquetiapine is the pharmacologically interesting active metabolite — NET inhibitor + 5-HT1A partial agonist.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 5-6x AUC increase — markedly higher sedation, hypotension, QT.
Major reduction in quetiapine exposure.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Histaminergic rebound: insomnia, anxiety, nausea on discontinuation, especially at sleep-aid doses.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Moderate QT prolongation, particularly in overdose.

notes: Off-label sleep aid usage exploits H1/α1 dominance at low doses — separate phenomenon from antipsychotic efficacy.

name: Diphenhydramine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: First-generation H1 — high CNS penetration (logP 3.3, no Pgp efflux). Inverse agonism vs neutral antagonism debate: clinical practice unaffected.
Anticholinergic activity drives deliriant effects in overdose.
Sernagor et al. — open-channel block of NMDA at micromolar conc; explains ketamine-like effects at very high doses.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triple-mechanism in overdose: H1 antagonism (sedation), anticholinergic (delirium, mydriasis, tachycardia), Na+ channel block (cardiotoxicity, QRS widening). The QRS/QT and seizures in overdose are sodium-channel-mediated and treated with sodium bicarbonate, mirroring TCA toxicity.

routes.notes: First-pass ~50% via CYP2D6, CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19. Elderly t1/2 doubled.

metabolism.notes: Also CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: DPH is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor (Ki ~1 μM)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Inhibits metoprolol, codeine, tamoxifen, antipsychotic metabolism.
Anticholinergic delirium; elderly especially vulnerable.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: PMs have higher exposure but the practical impact is small (broad therapeutic window).

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: H1 desensitisation within ~7-10 days of daily use → loss of sedative effect.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Overdose: QRS widening, QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia — TCA-like cardiotoxicity profile.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: ~2x t1/2; markedly increased delirium risk (Beers Criteria avoid).

notes: Major OTC sedative; cardiotoxicity profile in overdose underappreciated by the public.

name: Dimenhydrinate

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1:1 salt of diphenhydramine + 8-chlorotheophylline. Diphenhydramine free base is the active component (~55% by mass); 8-chlorotheophylline is a weak xanthine intended to offset diphenhydramine sedation. All pharmacology is DPH (see diphenhydramine entry).

notes: 8-chlorotheophylline is pharmacologically trivial at the doses used. See Diphenhydramine.

name: Dramamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trade name for dimenhydrinate. Note: 'Dramamine Less Drowsy' formulation actually contains meclizine, not dimenhydrinate.

notes: Trade name duplicate.

name: Hydroxyzine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Higher H1 affinity than diphenhydramine; metabolised to cetirizine.

binding.notes: 5-HT2A contributes to anxiolysis.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: H1 dominant sedation + 5-HT2A anxiolysis. Less anticholinergic than DPH. Major active metabolite = cetirizine (CYP3A4-mediated oxidation) — non-sedating peripheral H1 antagonist responsible for most steady-state H1 effect at the systemic level but not in CNS (cetirizine is P-gp substrate, low BBB penetration).

metabolism.notes: Cetirizine is itself a marketed antihistamine.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QT prolongation at high doses; FDA warning 2015.

notes: Useful anxiolytic in BZ-sparing protocols.

name: Cyclizine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: First-generation H1 + mild anticholinergic; antiemetic for motion sickness. Limited CNS penetration vs DPH.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~20 h. Hepatic N-demethylation to norcyclizine (active).

notes: Notable IV abuse potential (euphoria) recognised in palliative/perioperative settings.

name: Clonidine

binding.notes: Partial agonist (~70% Emax vs noradrenaline).

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Bousquet — I1 binding correlates better with antihypertensive potency than α2A binding; classical 'central sympatholytic' mechanism is now revised to include I1.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Central α2A presynaptic autoreceptor activation → reduced sympathetic outflow + I1 receptor activation in RVLM contributes. Used clinically for hypertension, ADHD (Kapvay), opioid/nicotine/alcohol withdrawal symptom relief.

routes.notes: t1/2 12-16 h. 40-60% renal unchanged.
Catapres-TTS weekly patch.

metabolism.notes: ~50% renal unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced antihypertensive efficacy.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe rebound hypertension on abrupt discontinuation (catecholamine surge); taper required.

notes: The I1 imidazoline receptor is poorly recognised in clinical pharmacology curricula — clonidine is the prototype I1 agonist.

name: Propranolol

primary_targets: β1 / β2 adrenergic (non-selective antagonist; S-(–)-enantiomer ~100x more potent)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: S-(–)-propranolol is the cardioactive enantiomer; R-(+) has membrane-stabilising effect.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective β-blocker; lipophilic, crosses BBB → useful for performance anxiety (peripheral somatic symptom suppression — tremor, tachycardia, sweating). Membrane-stabilising (Na+ channel) action at high conc explains overdose cardiotoxicity (similar to TCAs/cocaine).

routes.notes: Massive first-pass (~75%). t1/2 3-6 h IR. Hepatic CYP2D6 + CYP1A2 + CYP2C19. CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibitor (autoinhibition).

metabolism.notes: Mechanism-based inhibitor of CYP2D6 — autoinhibition contributes to dose-dependent nonlinear PK.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 30-50% lower exposure in smokers.
Reduced metabolism of co-administered CYP2D6 substrates.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs: higher exposure but offset by autoinhibition; PMs less common in clinical practice for dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Chronic β-blockade upregulates β-adrenergic receptors → rebound HTN/tachycardia on abrupt discontinuation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Rebound HTN/angina/MI risk on abrupt cessation; taper required.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Overdose: QRS widening, bradyarrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, seizures.

notes: Off-label use for performance anxiety leverages peripheral β-blockade rather than central anxiolysis.

name: Kava

functional.readout: potentiation of GABA currents in cortical neurons
functional.notes: Kavain, dihydrokavain, methysticin, dihydromethysticin, yangonin, desmethoxyyangonin all show modest GABA-A potentiation. Binding site distinct from BZ site (flumazenil insensitive).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Multi-target: 6 main kavalactones contribute. Anxiolytic activity primarily attributed to kavain and dihydrokavain via GABA-A non-BZ site PAM. Voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channel inhibition contributes to muscle relaxation and anticonvulsant effects.

routes.notes: Kavain t1/2 ~9 h after standard 200 mg extract.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Potentiates warfarin, midazolam, statins.
Liver failure case reports.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs may have higher hepatotoxicity risk due to altered kavalactone metabolism.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Rare fulminant hepatitis; 60+ case reports — leaf/stem-derived preparations and ethanol extraction implicated.

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative receptor binding for individual kavalactones
notes: Hepatotoxicity is the main safety concern; aqueous root preparations (traditional) are safer than ethanol/acetone extracts of aerial parts.

name: Kanna

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Mesembrine — the primary alkaloid — is a high-affinity SERT inhibitor (~SSRI-like) plus weak PDE4 inhibitor.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Misclassified as 'depressant' in this group — kanna's mesembrine alkaloids are SSRI-like, not GABAergic. Suggest reclassification.

routes.notes: Limited PK data.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome risk.

notes: Library classifies as depressant but mesembrine is SSRI-like. Should not be grouped with GABAergic depressants.

name: Ashwagandha

primary_targets: GABA-A (BZ site PAM by withanolides — weak)

functional.notes: Withaferin A and withanolides bind BZ-like site with weak affinity.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Multi-target adaptogen: withanolides modulate GABA-A, cortisol, NF-κB, and Nrf2/HO-1 signalling. Anxiolytic activity reproducibly demonstrated in clinical trials (Salve 2019, Lopresti 2019).

routes.notes: Withaferin A poorly characterised in humans.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Mild T4 elevation; not contraindicated in hypothyroidism but caution.

notes: Clinical anxiolytic effect modest but reproducible.

name: Marinol

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Dronabinol = synthetic Δ9-THC. Miscategorised here as GABAergic depressant; pharmacology is cannabinoid (see cannabinoids enrichment file).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Standard Δ9-THC pharmacology (CB1 partial agonism). See cannabinoids enrichment file.

routes.notes: Marinol = encapsulated dronabinol in sesame oil. F ~6-20% due to first-pass; high inter-individual variability.

notes: Miscategorised here as depressant; this is dronabinol (Δ9-THC). See cannabinoids enrichment file for full pharmacology.

name: Picamilon

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Soviet-era prodrug: GABA + niacin conjugate. Designed to cross BBB and dissociate centrally to GABA + nicotinic acid. Niacin causes cerebral vasodilation. Modest anxiolytic/cognitive effects in Russian literature; little Western validation.

routes.notes: Limited Western PK. FDA banned as supplement 2015.

notes: Soviet nootropic; mostly Russian-language data.

name: Gaba

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Exogenous oral GABA does NOT meaningfully cross the BBB (extremely polar zwitterion). Marketed supplement effects are largely placebo or via gut/enteric nervous system signalling. Any 'GABAergic' effect attributed to oral GABA supplements likely reflects bias.

routes.notes: BBB permeability very low; central effects not pharmacologically expected.

notes: Oral GABA supplements unlikely to produce direct central effects.

name: Fasoracetam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Racetam derivative. Originally developed by Nippon Shinyaku for vascular dementia; failed Phase III. Investigated for ADHD with mGluR-network gene variants (Aevi Medical). Mechanism: chronic dosing upregulates mGluR2/3 and GABA-B in rats — no validated acute receptor binding.

routes.notes: Short t1/2 ~1.5 h.

notes: Mechanism poorly characterised; clinical efficacy unproven.

name: Pagoclone

primary_targets: GABA-A α2β2γ2 (subunit-selective partial agonist at BZ site)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Cyclopyrrolone (related to zopiclone). Partial agonist with α2/α3 selectivity → anxiolytic without sedation in animal models.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclopyrrolone partial agonist at BZ site; developed for anxiety and panic disorder, later investigated for stuttering. Failed Phase III. Subunit-selective PAM concept similar to subtype-selective bretazenil.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Possible BZ-like, attenuated by partial agonism.

notes: Discontinued. Notable for the (failed) subtype-selectivity concept.

name: Ronlax

primary_targets: GABA-A (BZ site PAM, via desethyl active metabolite)
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ester prodrug of descarboxyloflazepate; cleaved by gut/liver esterases to active long-acting BZ. See benzos enrichment file for class pharmacology.

routes.notes: Active metabolite t1/2 ~70-100 h.

notes: Benzodiazepine prodrug; see benzos enrichment file.

name: Fosazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Water-soluble diazepam analog with phosphono group at N-1. Pro-drug-like in vivo conversion to diazepam-like activity. See benzos file.

notes: Obscure water-soluble BZ.

name: Flubrotizolam

class_name: Other GABAergic depressants (alcohol, GHB family, gabapentinoids, phenibut, baclofen, barbiturates, quinazolinones)
shared_mechanism: This is a heterogeneous group united by clinical CNS depressant effect rather than a shared receptor target. Mechanisms diverge wildly: (1) Ethanol acts at NMDA (channel blocker, IC50 ~50 mM), GABA-A δ-subunit, glycine receptors, 5-HT3, nAChR, GIRK — and indirectly via neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) induction. (2) GHB has a high-affinity 'GHB receptor' (Maitre site, ~580 nM) plus low-affinity GABA-B partial agonism (~200 μM) — this dual-site pharmacology underlies the biphasic dose response (low dose stimulant, high dose sedative-coma). GBL and 1,4-butanediol are GHB prodrugs (lactonase and ADH/ALDH respectively). (3) Gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) are NOT GABA receptor ligands despite the name — they bind the α2δ-1 auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, reducing presynaptic Ca2+ entry and transmitter release. Pregabalin has ~6x higher α2δ-1 affinity than gabapentin. (4) Phenibut combines GABA-B partial agonism (like baclofen) with weak α2δ binding (like gabapentin) — a dual mechanism shared with no other widely used compound. (5) Baclofen is the prototype selective GABA-B agonist (R1/R2 obligate heterodimer). (6) Barbiturates bind a β+/α- pocket on GABA-A and at high concentrations DIRECTLY open the chloride channel without GABA — this distinguishes them from benzodiazepines and explains higher overdose lethality. (7) Methaqualone-family quinazolinones bind the etomidate/propofol pocket on GABA-A (distinct from both BZ and barbiturate sites).
shared_pk_summary: PK varies dramatically. Ethanol: zero-order elimination via ADH (Km ~2 mM = ~0.02 g/dL BAC), inducible CYP2E1 minor path. GHB: capacity-limited absorption AND elimination, dose-dependent t1/2 (~30-90 min), 95% metabolised to succinate via SSADH (Krebs cycle). Gabapentin: saturable LAT1 absorption (F% drops 60→25% across 300→3600 mg), 100% renal unchanged. Pregabalin: linear PK, 98% renal unchanged. Phenibut: ~65% renal unchanged, t1/2 ~5 h. Baclofen: 70-85% renal unchanged, t1/2 2-6 h PO. Barbiturates: extensive hepatic CYP oxidation, very long t1/2 (phenobarb ~100 h, pentobarb ~20 h), PXR/CAR pan-CYP inducers. Methaqualone: lipophilic, large Vd, hepatic clearance.
shared_safety: Universal feature: dose-dependent respiratory depression. Synergy with other GABA-A PAMs (BZs, Z-drugs), opioids, and ethanol → leading cause of accidental overdose death. Barbiturates lethal via direct GABA-A channel opening at supratherapeutic doses (no ceiling). Gabapentinoids implicated in opioid-overdose deaths (UK Schedule 3 reclassification 2019). Withdrawal mechanisms: GABA-A downregulation + NMDA upregulation (ethanol, BZs, barbiturates) → seizures, delirium tremens. GABA-B receptor downregulation (GHB, phenibut, chronic baclofen) → protracted withdrawal with psychiatric sequelae. GHB has a narrow therapeutic index (sedative dose ~250-500 μM brain conc; coma at 600-800 μM).
sar_summary: GABA-B: β-aryl GABA scaffold (phenibut → baclofen p-chloro → 4-F phenibut). para-chloro (baclofen) gives highest selectivity and potency; para-F (4-F phenibut) gives lipophilicity boost + duration. α2δ ligands: β-amino acid scaffold, cyclohexyl ring (gabapentin) vs isobutyl (pregabalin) vs bicyclic (mirogabalin). Pregabalin's stereochemistry and methyl branching give ~6x α2δ-1 affinity boost. Barbiturates: 5,5-disubstitution at the pyrimidinetrione ring; alkyl side chains (pentobarb) give anaesthesia (higher direct activation), aryl side chain (phenobarb) gives anticonvulsant efficacy with less direct activation. Quinazolinones (methaqualone, mecloqualone, etaqualone, mebroqualone, methylmethaqualone, SL-164): substitution on the 3-aryl group and the 2-methyl/ethyl modulates potency at the etomidate-site GABA-A pocket. GHB analogues: 4-OH on butyric acid is essential; GBL (lactone) is prodrug; 1,4-BD (diol) is two-step prodrug.

name: Tizanidine

metabolism.notes: Near-complete presystemic CYP1A2 metabolism (oral bioavailability ~34% from extensive first-pass; only ~2.7% excreted unchanged). Clearance is CYP1A2-dominated, so strong CYP1A2 inhibitors cause very large PK interactions: fluvoxamine raised tizanidine AUC ~33-fold (range 14-103x) with SBP falling to ~79-80 mmHg (Granfors 2004, PMID 15060511); ciprofloxacin raised AUC ~10-fold (Granfors 2004, PMID 15536460). FDA-contraindicated with fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin; CYP1A2 induction by tobacco smoking lowers tizanidine exposure.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: CYP1A2 inhibition (tizanidine is a near-exclusive CYP1A2 substrate)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Tizanidine AUC +33x, severe hypotension and sedation; FDA-contraindicated.
Tizanidine AUC +10x, marked hypotension; FDA-contraindicated.
